extracted.intended_audience: efficiency review (ER) teams, Department of Defense medical managers, policymakers, and researchers evaluating military medical outpatient services
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for conducting Efficiency Review (ER) of military outpatient clinics, covering data sources, case-mix/DRG approaches, cost measurement, performance-measure design, and practical limitations. Intended to help ER teams assess utilization, productivity, and possible reforms in military medical delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine why patients seek outpatient care / define legitimate care
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing the ER team would want to know is why patients seek outpatient medical care: this is because the ER team would need to know what legitimate care is--to determine what should or should not be seen at the outpatient facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify patient service requirements from both the patient perspective and the practitioner's perspective. Use Donabedian's phenomena (people; mortality/survival; morbidity; situations requiring care but not classifiable as morbidity or mortality; health) to structure what constitutes service-requiring potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donabedian's service-requiring factors
rubrics_metrics.description: "1) people, 2) mortality or survival, 3) morbidity, 4) situations that require care, but which cannot be classified as morbidity or mortality, ... health" (Donabedian)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five dimensions as a conceptual checklist when determining what outpatient visits legitimately require services and therefore should be counted as appropriate utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient demographics validity and DEERS catchment considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use DEERS to obtain demographic data for populations eligible for the Uniformed Services Health Care Delivery System, including catchment-area beneficiary estimates, but recognize the DEERS data are new and imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cautions enumerated include: 1) DEERS is relatively new and error-prone; 2) serious questions about input validity exist and careful verification is required; 3) patient demographics differ markedly by location; 4) patients are generally free to seek outpatient care outside an MTF; 5) some inpatient care is provided under CHAMPUS; 6) patients outside catchment areas are not required to use the MTF; 7) active duty beneficiaries are transient; 8) satellite outpatient treatment demographics are aggregated into parent MTF reports and may not be available separately. ER teams must account for these limitations when using DEERS or catchment estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortality data for utilization adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortality (survival) is relevant because mortality rates are used to adjust incidence rates for utilization analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware Department of Defense collects mainly deaths occurring in military facilities; other sources (e.g., DEERS) may supply additional but incomplete data. Local mortality figures are often unavailable and this limits certain adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morbidity and incidence measurement (disease characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidence rates are the most important aspect of morbidity for utilization measurement; disease complexity, duration, and intensity also influence care-seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local morbidity characteristics differ by catchment area and are generally unavailable at the local level for ER purposes. Where possible, characterize incidence, complexity, duration, and intensity to inform expected resource consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case-mix (DRG) approaches to measure output
rubrics_metrics.description: A case-mix scheme (DRGs) aggregates patients with similar cases into groups that define case-mix in terms of percentage of patients in each grouping; linkage of case-mix to resource-mix produces a determinable cost-mix and a stable distribution of resource use for product definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DRGs should: represent patient types/intensities/durations; place patients into a manageable number of classes representative of resource-consumption patterns; permit cost-mix determination. Recognize DRG benefits (useful for regional utilization review; standards for prospective reimbursement; planning/budgeting; efficiency measures; patient profiles for scheduling) and limitations (local/regional variation, not based on actual patient costs but averages, limited variables due to data availability, influenced by time/resource changes, subjective judgments). To develop DRG-based cost data, follow steps: group hospitals, collect patient demographic/clinical/cost data, assign DRGs, calculate average cost per DRG, compute average across DRGs and hospitals, compute hospital-specific expected costs by DRG mix, sum to get hospital index and compare to averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for outpatient-specific case-mix groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been little effort to develop DRGs or Ambulatory Care Groupings for outpatient visits; outpatient classification requires sufficient independent variables to capture intensity, complexity, duration and permit clear resource-allocation patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ER teams should recognize the difficulty of defining outpatient case-mix and consider development or adaptation of classification schemes (e.g., AUTOGRP) suitable for ambulatory data, ensuring sufficient granularity to reflect resource use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize visits not defined by morbidity/mortality (administrative/preventive/mission-driven)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roughly one-half of beneficiaries visit clinics for reasons other than disease (hypochondriasis, administrative paperwork, preventive care like prenatal/well-baby, social counseling, required physicals for duty-related permits, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for these non-disease visit types in utilization analysis rather than assuming all visits reflect morbidity-driven demand. Different appointment/scheduling strategies and resource assignments may be appropriate for these visit types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health status measurement is complex and local data lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Health status has many definitions; some use quantitative measures (days lost from work) but military sources often lack data collection methods that define or reflect local catchment health status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential measures useful to ER analysts include utilization rates, workdays lost, morbidity and mortality rates; however, local availability is limited and ER teams should plan for data collection or use proxy measures cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: ER must verify acceptable quality standards before efficiency actions (DODI 5010.XX)
rubrics_metrics.description: DODI 5010.XX and other directives require that the ER process must ensure the activity being analyzed currently has acceptable quality standards and that output must meet those standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess existence and functioning of peer/utilization review standards, professional credentialing, patient profile standards, facility/personnel standards, safety standards, etc. Identification, implementation, acceptance and use of quality standards are necessary preconditions before cost-containment measures are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost data must be relatable, timely, and traceable to activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Uniform Chart of Accounts provides consistent cost reporting but has problems: information is not directly relatable to individual patients, provides average costs allocated through stepped-down methods, and is often six months old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ER teams should seek cost information that can be traced to the activity or patient group where possible, consider problems of allocation and lag, and include standby/contingency costs (facility, staffing, equipment) when estimating 'true' cost. Determine which perspective(s) of cost (government, beneficiary, societal) will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance measure design guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Several generally accepted guidelines for measures are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measures to: 1) avoid perverse or negative incentives for the entity measured; 2) avoid manipulative potential of input variables; 3) rely on inputs that are available, easily identified and representative of actual inputs; 4) be relatively simple to implement, use, and understand; 5) produce single-valued, understandable results; 6) be inexpensive and not labor intensive; 7) eliminate as much subjectivity as possible from inputs; and 8) avoid any reference to quality of performance (for this efficiency measure specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate costs with performance; cost-per-beneficiary preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures should associate costs with performance; common relationships are (a) cost per population, (b) cost per output, and (c) cost/percentage relationships. Any measure developed probably should reflect cost per beneficiary or cost per patient episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages of cost-per-beneficiary: commonality across different service measures (avoids differences among outpatient visits, occupied bed days, etc.), not easily manipulated by the measured activity, avoids perverse incentives. Disadvantages: does not fully explain drivers of demand and cost; inclusion of cost per output can suffer from many surrogate labels and manipulation. Choose and document the relationship used and be aware of tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case-mix adjustment rather than crude aggregate outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional single-value representations (outpatient visit, patient day) are 'crude'; literature advocates measuring output on the basis of case-mix adjusted patient visit or patient day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust outputs for case-mix to better reflect differing resource needs across patient types. Where case-mix adjustment is not possible, recognize the limitations and potential biases of crude proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions to improve representation of MTF productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If made common by DOD requirements, certain conditions would greatly improve representation of MTF productivity by proxy measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desirable conditions include: uniformity of MTF data and definitions of variables/characteristics; full-cost identification and recognition (center definition, full cost identification); uniformity of non-direct patient care cost isolation; capability to trace costs to actual groupings of patients receiving services (DRGs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-grouping to achieve comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: For lack of a better scheme, medical facilities are commonly grouped by variables intended to bring homogeneity to groupings (peer grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical variables for clustering include hospital size (beds), number and types of services offered, presence of teaching/residency programs, number of admissions, etc. Use linear regression or cluster analysis to form peer groups for comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define reference point/base of comparison before measuring productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: A major problem has been the development of a common measure and a defined base of comparison or reference point; Clinic A and Clinic B may not be comparable unless the base is appropriately defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish what the comparator is (peer group average, regional standard, historical baseline) and ensure adjustments (case-mix, demographics, mission differences) are applied so comparisons are meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider interdependencies and potential harms of policy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of locale, population, structure, policy, etc., make measurement and reform complex; policy changes (e.g., access modification or nuisance fees) can harm legitimate usage, morale, or retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before imposing controls to reduce assumed over-utilization, evaluate how controls will affect legitimate care-seeking, active duty morale/retention, and unintended consequences. ER teams must weigh benefits against possible harms and system interdependencies.
